observation.visible_scene: Extreme close-up of a glossy, translucent orange dome-shaped object sitting on a bed of fine white granules. The dome's wet surface carries bright specular highlights (a pale crescent near the top and a small white blob on the right), and its lower rim is fringed with the white granules.
visible_changes: Over the excerpt the white granules clinging to the dome's lower rim gradually become coated with a thin translucent amber liquid that seeps out at the base and spreads laterally into the surrounding granules, darkening/wetting that band while the granules farther out stay dry and white.
The dome's bottom contour, initially a fairly crisp wavy edge with adhering granules, becomes smoother and more diffuse as the liquid halo grows.

The specular highlights on the surface (top crescent and right-side blob) slowly change shape and position—e.g., the right highlight elongates into a streak mid-clip and later splits—consistent with a deforming/melting wet surface rather than separate objects moving.
A thin pale squiggly reflection on the left side of the dome shifts slightly in form over time.

The overall size and centered position of the dome within the frame remain broadly constant; the dominant change is the spreading liquid and the reshaping highlights, not a large translation of the body.
Early frames (roughly 1–10) show little visible change beyond minor highlight drift, indicating a slow, near-steady onset of the liquid seepage that becomes more evident in later frames.
outside_clip_unknowns: The cause of the liquid appearing at the base and the identity/material of both the dome and the white granules are not shown.
What happens before the first frame (whether the dome was already softening) and the final outcome after the last frame (full collapse, continued pooling, etc.) are unknown.
Whether the granules are merely being wetted or are also dissolving cannot be determined from the visible frames.
uncertain_details: Camera motion is uncertain: the framing of the dome is nearly constant, so the subtle apparent shift of the top highlight could be either a slight camera drift/zoom or genuine surface deformation.
Distinguishing the dome's own slow sag/flattening from the growing liquid halo at its base is not fully resolvable at this resolution.
